text.p: This is the year you will most likely start shopping online, if you haven't already. As the bigger names in retailing head to the Internet, so will modem-equipped shoppers with more dimes than time.

By the year 2000, expect $7.3 billion in online commerce a year, according to New York research firm Jupiter Communications. This year, Jupiter expects online merchants to download $2.3 billion in transactions from their pioneering customers.

The prospect of online shopping poses two different challenges for consumers: You have to guard your transactions from the prying keystrokes of larcenous hackers, and you have to make sure you don't spend even more money than you already do on stupid stuff you don't really need.

The good news is that there are positive developments on both fronts. Mastercard and Visa have just announced new developments in their pilot projects to safeguard electronic transactions including online checks and credit card purchases.

CyberCash, the Reston, Va., upstart, has unveiled an electronic check transaction system as well as CyberCoin -- an online system that will allow you to spend as little as 25 cents in an online transaction that is secured. Many Internet service providers have added credit card encryption programmes to their sites.
"As soon as they feel that their cash is safe, virtually everyone with a computer will be accessing online stores," says Gerald Celente, author of Trends 2000 (Warner Books, 1977, $24.).
Many of those transactions are already safe -- if someone steals your credit card number, your liability is limited just as if someone stole your credit card on the street.

Electronic transfers -- such as online checks or coins, which debit your bank account when you make an online transaction -- are protected by Federal Reserve rules that limit consumer liability if money is electronically transferred in error or crime.
So how do you make the most of the online malls? Here are some tips.
-- Start with credit cards first. If the highly unlikely does occur, it's easier to straighten out a mess in your credit card account than one in your checkbook.
-- Start with a big name merchant, if for no other reason than the comfort factor. You know who they are and where they are, besides at www.something.

-- Shop commodities, which may include items you never thought of as commodities before. Books are big, tires will be too, says Celente. Go slow ordering clothing or other personal items you may want to return -- it's no easier to pack up and reship a cyber-item than a mail order one.
-- Remember that no-free-lunch rule? Expect that as electronic money becomes more widely used, you'll end up paying for items that were previously free on the Internet.

Quality investment data already comes at a price, if you want to consume timely and significant volumes of it. As merchants find out what kind of information and entertainment you're willing to pay for, expect to be asked for the cash.

Maybe it won't be the in-depth provocative analysis that Slate magazine offers, and is having a hard time selling. How about instantaneous e-mail when there's an O.J. verdict or Michael Jackson's kid is born? (Not that many people will admit to paying for this stuff, but look at the success of Entertainment Tonight and People magazine. You can buy it really anonymously online).

-- Enjoy the show. Think about where online spending makes the most sense: Travel arrangements, where you can preview an area you've never been to before, or make your own competitive airline reservations, already consume almost one of every two online dollars spent. Why not buy CDs where you can preview the music first and then buy at a discount, without leaving your desk?
Celente envisions a day when you can shop online for a refrigerator and virtually stock it with the food you have on hand, just to see how it fits.

-- Enjoy the competition. Today, Amazon books offers more than a million titles, hardcovers at 30 percent off, and entertaining insights from the authors and reviewers. Tomorrow, maybe it will be Barnes & Noble or Borders.

If there was any vestige of retailer loyalty left in you, forget it: The barriers to entry, as they say in the business, are so low online that anybody could throw up a virtual store. The rent is cheap, and there's no need for big inventories. Shop price and shop service.

-- Avoid traps. Right now, reputable online stores are going out of the way to make sure you don't buy anything by mistake. But it's only a short step to the kind of negative checkoffs which already stuff your paper mail box: Avoid signing up for anything online (other than your basic online service) which offers to deduct from your credit card in perpetuity. Once you sign a release like that, you've given away a lot of ground.
